title: Inhibitory Plasticity and E/I Balance

html:
The voltage/Ca2+^{2+}-dependent and three-factor mechanisms introduced above were developed mainly in the context of excitatory plasticity, but cortical learning is not stabilized by excitation alone. In cortex, inhibitory synapses are themselves plastic, excitatory drive onto interneurons is plastic, and both are required to keep learned changes from saturating or destabilizing the circuit 1, 2, 3. Inhibitory synapses are therefore not passive scaffolding; they are part of cortical credit assignment and part of the machinery that keeps learned representations usable rather than runaway. In mouse hippocampal CA1, learning-related inhibitory-synapse remodeling differs between dendrites and the axon initial segment (Figure) 21. Longitudinal imaging compares inhibitory synapse turnover across CA1 compartments (Figure).

It is useful to separate three levels of claim. First, the canonical theoretical principle is well established: inhibitory plasticity can homeostatically restore E/I balance and stabilize cortical dynamics, as in the Vogels-type framework where inhibitory weights adapt to maintain sparse, asynchronous, stable activity 4. Second, specific cortical rules have been demonstrated for particular pathways, including I→\toE and E→\toI synapses with pathway- and cell-type-specific LTP, LTD, and STDP 2. Third, and importantly, there is no single cortex-wide inhibitory learning rule analogous to the simplified textbook picture often given for excitatory STDP; the effective rule depends strongly on interneuron subtype, postsynaptic target compartment, induction protocol, and modulatory context.

The cleanest theoretical starting point is therefore the homeostatic inhibitory-plasticity picture, not a claim that every cortical inhibitory synapse literally obeys one symmetric STDP law. In recurrent-network models, inhibitory plasticity provides negative feedback that can establish and maintain balanced excitation and inhibition, yielding stable asynchronous states while preserving learned structure 4, 5. This is the right organizing principle for cortex: inhibitory plasticity is the main anti-runaway mechanism that lets excitatory learning occur safely.

At I→\toE synapses, a useful unifying point is that inhibitory plasticity is often gated by postsynaptic pyramidal-cell Ca2+^{2+} arising from excitatory mechanisms such as NMDAR activation, voltage-gated Ca2+ channel recruitment, and backpropagating spikes, rather than from the GABAergic synapse alone 6. This makes inhibitory plasticity inherently context-dependent on the surrounding excitatory state. But beyond that shared dependence, cortical I→\toE rules are highly diverse: cortical inhibitory synapses can show timing-dependent bidirectional change, burst-triggered potentiation, and heterosynaptic reweighting rather than one uniform iSTDP law 2, 3.

A strong empirical anchor is the D’Amour and Froemke result in mouse auditory cortex. Pairing presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes potentiated inhibition within an approximately ±10\pm 10 ms window regardless of precise order, whereas co-recorded excitatory inputs followed a more classical asymmetric STDP window 7; both depended on NMDAR activation, and together they adjusted the E/I ratio, tightened the E-I lag, and improved spike-timing fidelity. The symmetry of the inhibitory rule makes functional sense: if the job of inhibitory plasticity is to rapidly bring co-active inhibition into register with the excitatory events that drive postsynaptic spiking, then any inhibitory input that reliably participates in that narrow peri-spike window should strengthen whether it slightly leads or slightly follows the spike. That is best read as a timing-alignment and gain-normalization rule, not as a mirror image of excitatory Hebbian STDP.

Another major cortical result is PV/perisomatic LTPi in neocortical layer 5. Postsynaptic depolarization or brief bursts in pyramidal neurons can selectively potentiate perisomatic inhibition from PV basket cells without changing nearby glutamatergic input; this plasticity depends on postsynaptic Ca2+^{2+}, NMDARs, L-type Ca2+^{2+} channels, and retrograde nitric-oxide signaling, increases presynaptic GABA release, and narrows the temporal integration window of the pyramidal neuron 8. This is another clear example of inhibitory plasticity implementing gain normalization and temporal precision control.

The broader I→\toE (inhibitory→\toexcitatory) frontier is that different inhibitory projection classes almost certainly obey different effective rules matched to their circuit roles. PV→\topyramidal synapses are positioned to regulate perisomatic gain and spike timing; SST→\topyramidal synapses gate distal and apical dendrites; chandelier cells target the axon initial segment; and disinhibitory motifs change whether dendritic coincidence is even allowed to matter. The reviews are quite clear that the field does not yet support a single settled cortex-wide taxonomy for all of these pathways, so the safest summary is diversity constrained by compartmental function 2, 3, 9.

Plasticity at E→\toI synapses is the other half of cortical E/I balancing: learning changes not only how much inhibition pyramidal neurons receive, but how strongly excitation recruits each interneuron class. Here the dominant empirical principle is extreme target-cell specificity. In L2/3 somatosensory cortex, pyramidal→\toLTS synapses (LTS=low-threshold spiking cell; often SST) show bidirectional STDP, whereas pyramidal→\toFS synapses (FS=fast-spiking cell; often PV) show only LTD under the same pairing protocols 10; mechanistically, LTP at pyramidal→\toLTS depends on postsynaptic NMDARs, whereas LTD depends on mGluRs. So even when the presynaptic cell is the same pyramidal neuron, the plasticity rule depends sharply on interneuron identity.

Additional E→\toI results reinforce this picture. In mouse V1, theta-burst stimulation paired with depolarization preferentially induces LTP at excitatory synapses onto fast-spiking interneurons, but this LTP is NMDAR-independent and voltage-gated Ca2+ channel-independent, instead requiring postsynaptic Ca2+^{2+} elevation via mGluR5-driven release from internal stores 11. By contrast, excitatory synapses onto neocortical SST interneurons can express a strong-stimulation LTP that is presynaptic in expression, NMDAR-independent, insensitive to postsynaptic Ca2+^{2+} chelation (suppression), and dependent on cAMP/PKA signaling 12. So the main lesson of cortical E→\toI plasticity is not a universal postsynaptic Ca2+^{2+} rule, but extreme subtype-specificity in how plasticity is induced. Some interneuron classes use postsynaptic Ca2+^{2+} rises reached through distinct routes, whereas others can express LTP that is NMDAR-independent and insensitive to postsynaptic Ca2+^{2+} chelation 11, 12.

In general, the strongest modern framing is thus not “excitation learns first, inhibition compensates afterward,” but that local excitatory and inhibitory synapses are often co-trained. In mouse auditory cortex, pairing protocols can modify both paired excitatory and paired inhibitory inputs while also inducing heterosynaptic changes at the strongest unpaired inputs; these coordinated changes require dendritic Ca2+^{2+} signaling and set a cell-specific E/I correlation set-point 13. Complementing that, work in visual cortex shows that inhibitory plasticity can directly alter the sign and capacity of excitatory plasticity at the same postsynaptic neuron 14. So inhibition is not merely downstream stabilization; it actively helps determine the admissible regime for excitatory learning. A model links excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity (Figure). The model also investigates excitation–inhibition balance (Figure).

A useful theoretical synthesis is therefore the co-dependent plasticity picture: excitatory and inhibitory synapses should be treated as a coupled local learning system rather than two separate subsystems 6. In that view, inhibitory strength gates whether excitatory potentiation is possible, neighboring excitatory interactions shape LTP magnitude, and heterosynaptic redistribution stabilizes the result; together these mechanisms allow fast learning without long-term instability 6. That specific formalism is theoretical rather than a direct experimental law, but it captures the direction in which the cortical data point: a dendritic branch or local input ensemble is often best treated as a coupled E/I learning unit.

Inhibitory plasticity also operates across slower timescales. Transient disinhibition often opens a cortical plasticity window, whereas slower inhibitory reweighting helps close that window again and restore a stable operating point. In adult neocortex, inhibitory circuits are structurally plastic as well as electrophysiologically plastic: chronic imaging and review work show experience-dependent branch remodeling, bouton turnover, and circuit-specific restructuring of inhibitory connections 15, 16, 17. At an even slower "metaplastic" scale, activity-dependent transcriptional programs such as NPAS4 promote inhibitory synapse formation onto excitatory neurons and, through cell-type-specific gene programs, can also increase excitation onto inhibitory neurons 18, 19; BDNF-related pathways are likewise major regulators of inhibitory-circuit maturation and critical-period timing 20.

Overall, inhibitory plasticity makes cortical learning selective, stable, and precise: it does not simply oppose excitation, but co-defines which excitatory changes are allowed, how sharply they are expressed, and in what dynamical regime they remain usable 4, 14, 7.
